query: Which adversarial attack models (poisoning rates, backdoor trigger types, trigger placement/strength) and generation pipelines produce reproducible robustness benchmarks for detectors and recovery strategies?

response.query: Which adversarial attack models (poisoning rates, backdoor trigger types, trigger placement/strength) and generation pipelines produce reproducible robustness benchmarks for detectors and recovery strategies?
response.answer: Backdoor attacks use poisoned data with triggers, while data poisoning focuses on stealthily influencing model training. Common triggers include images or text patterns. Robustness benchmarks often use gradient-based attacks for evaluation.

results.title: RAB: Provable Robustness Against Backdoor Attacks | Request PDF
results.content: Similar to Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), backdoor attacks in GNNs lie in the fact that the attacker modifies a portion of graph data by embedding triggers and enforces the model to learn the trigger feature during the model training process. Extensive experimental evaluations on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that GCleaner can reduce the backdoor attack success rate to 10% with only 1% of clean data, and has almost negligible degradation in model performance, which far outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) defense methods. However, its distributed nature makes it vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries manipulate training data or model updates to trigger attacker-chosen outputs. Backdoor attacks are a form of adversarial attacks on deep networks where the attacker provides poisoned data to the victim to train the model with, and then activates the attack by showing a specific small trigger pattern at the test time. Different from all existing work, our studied poisoning strategies can apply under a very weak threat model: (1) the adversary has no knowledge of the model and the training set used by the victim system; (2) the attacker is allowed to inject only a small amount of poisoning samples; (3) the backdoor key is hard to notice even by human beings to achieve stealthiness. Backdoor attacks are a form of adversarial attacks on deep networks where the attacker provides poisoned data to the victim to train the model with, and then activates the attack by showing a specific small trigger pattern at the test time. Data poisoning is a type of adversarial attack on machine learning models wherein the attacker adds examples to the training set to manipulate the behavior of the model at test time. Although poisoning attack against support vector machines (SVM) has been extensively studied before, there is still very limited knowledge about how such attack can be implemented on neural networks (NN), especially DNNs. In this work, we first examine the possibility of applying traditional gradient-based method (named as the direct gradient method) to generate poisoned data against NNs by leveraging the gradient of the target model w.r.t. the normal data.

results.title: (PDF) UniGuardian: A Unified Defense for Detecting Prompt Injection, Backdoor Attacks and Adversarial Attacks in Large Language Models
results.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to attacks like prompt injection, backdoor attacks, and adversarial attacks, which manipulate prompts or models to generate harmful outputs. In this paper, departing from traditional deep learning attack paradigms, we explore their intrinsic relationship and collectively term them Prompt Trigger Attacks (PTA). To address this, we propose UniGuardian, the first unified defense mechanism designed to detect prompt injection, backdoor attacks, and adversarial attacks in LLMs. Additionally, we introduce a single-forward strategy to optimize the detection pipeline, enabling simultaneous attack detection and text generation within a single forward pass.
